title: Bonding, Structure and Properties
seo_title: Year 10 Science: Bonding, Structure and Properties Worksheets (GCSE Combined Science)
standard_code: KS4 Chemistry: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
standard_text: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding; the formation of ions and ionic compounds and their formulae; the three states of matter and changes of state; the properties of ionic compounds, small molecules, polymers, giant covalent structures and metals and alloys; diamond, graphite, graphene and fullerenes; how structure and bonding explain melting and boiling points and electrical conductivity.
meta_desc: Free Year 10 GCSE Combined Science worksheets on bonding and structure: ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, formulae, giant lattices, simple molecules, diamond, graphite and graphene. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Structure explains melting point and conductivity.
key_sub: Ionic: transfer electrons. Covalent: share electrons. Metallic: sea of electrons.
body_html:
How to think about it

The type of bonding decides a substance's properties.

  • Ionic (metal + non-metal): giant lattice, high melting point, conducts only when molten or dissolved.
  • Covalent (non-metals): small molecules with low melting points, or giant covalent structures such as diamond and graphite.
  • Metallic: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, so metals conduct and are malleable.
Example

Na⁺ and O²⁻. Formula?

Two Na⁺ balance one O²⁻

Answer: Na₂O

Example

Low melting point, does not conduct. Structure?

Weak forces between molecules

Answer: simple molecules

Common mistakes

  • Thinking ionic compounds conduct when solid.
  • Thinking melting a simple molecule breaks covalent bonds.
  • Thinking graphite cannot conduct.

faq.q: What is the difference between ionic and covalent bonding?
faq.a: In ionic bonding electrons are transferred from metal to non-metal atoms, forming ions. In covalent bonding non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons.

faq.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
faq.a: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move. In diamond all four outer electrons are in bonds.

faq.q: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting points?
faq.a: Only the weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome; the strong covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break.

items.q: How many covalent bonds does phosphorus (P) usually form?
items.e: It needs 3 more electrons for a full outer shell.

items.q: Phosphorus (P) has 5 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 3 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 3 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: What happens in ionic bonding?
c: Electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, making oppositely charged ions.
Electrons are delocalised in a metal.
items.e: Metal + non-metal.

items.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
c: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in all directions need lots of energy to overcome.
items.e: Giant lattice.

items.q: What is metallic bonding?
c: attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons
transfer of electrons to a non-metal
items.e: Explains conductivity.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between fluorine (F) and iodine (I)?

items.q: What kind of bond forms between chlorine (Cl) and hydrogen (H)?

items.q: What kind of bond forms between magnesium (Mg) and sodium (Na)?

items.q: What happens in covalent bonding?
c: Electrons move freely in a sea.
Non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons.
items.e: Non-metal + non-metal.

items.q: Oxygen (O) has 6 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 2 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 2 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between zinc (Zn) and oxygen (O)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: Sulfur (S) has 6 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 2 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 2 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: Why does melting a simple molecular substance need little energy?
c: The molecules break apart into atoms.
Only the weak forces between molecules are overcome, not the covalent bonds.
items.e: Intermolecular forces.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>) or sodium chloride (NaCl)?
c: They boil at the same temperature.
It depends only on the container.
items.e: Sodium chloride has ionic attractions, which are stronger than the intermolecular forces in octane.

items.q: List from lowest to highest boiling point: bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>), fluorine (F<sub>2</sub>), iodine (I<sub>2</sub>).
items.e: All have only intermolecular forces; more electrons (larger molar mass) means stronger forces.
